relevance_note: Single-patient case report of a woman with a GFAP deletion and Alexander disease: "This individual has a large heterozygous deletion (exons 1–9) in the GFAP gene, so the case suffered from Alexander disease."
method_note: Read the whole paper by hand; no tables in the paper; a Python script only assembled the JSON from values I read, and every span was checked verbatim by script. Scope: the index patient ('patient'); two relatives described in the family history with clinical details (brother, daughter; neither tested nor said to have Alexander disease, included as relatives described in relation to the patient); two previously published individuals in the Discussion with individual-level facts (Melchionda et al.,2013 case: features; Zaver & Douthit 2019 case: sex, age, features, missense GFAP variant without printed description). Not included: Lichtenstein et al. 2017 three siblings (suspected AOAD confirmed only with MRI; features described only at group level), Pareyson (11 cases) and Balbi (112 cases) series (group level only), Green et al. 2018 exon 5 deletion (no individual-level fact), and the patient's father, father-in-law, husband and son (no clinical detail relevant beyond death/cirrhosis). No GFAP variant row for the Melchionda case: the text says only 'genetically confirmed as Alexander disease' and names no gene or variant for that person. Contradiction: the MRI section says 'AOAD involved the anterior part of frontal lobes ... with regard to white matter', while the Discussion says 'frontal white matter involvement was absent'; both rows emitted. The checklist item 'cerebral white matter abnormality' is still observed from the separate periventricular white matter findings and 'white matter hyperintensity in MRI'. Temporal, not contradictory: 'Physical and neurological examination was normal' (at the first admission after the suicide attempt at 50) precedes the later abnormal neurological examination (hyperreflexia, spasticity, Hoffman's sign); recorded as an excluded row 'abnormal physical and neurological examination' as the paper words it, excluding nothing more specific. Likewise 'normal cognitive function' after discharge, followed by cognitive impairment months later; both rows emitted, checklist cognitive decline observed. 'Blood and urine workup ... all came back normal' recorded as excluded 'abnormal blood and urine workup' without specifying analytes. 'Other examinations showed no abnormalities' was not used to exclude anything. Age at onset 'at the age of 35' is the onset of depression, which the authors present as the probable psychiatric onset of the disease ('her initial manifestation was probably psychiatric'); hedged by the authors. Age 52 is the age at report; no age at diagnosis is stated. Vital status of the patient not stated explicitly. Pathogenicity recorded as the authors' 'novel mutation'; their haploinsufficiency reasoning is speculation, not a functional assay, so functional evidence is 'not reported'. Brother's age '60-year-old' recorded as age at last evaluation (not stated whether it is age at death). Tremor, headache and nausea are reported as adverse effects of antidepressants.
